corpus.title: LatticeDB Embedded Property-Graph Architecture
corpus.text: LatticeDB is a serverless, embedded property-graph database designed for high-performance in-process execution. Operating similarly to SQLite for graph and vector data, LatticeDB eliminates remote database network boundaries by running entirely inside the host application process. It uniquely unites Cypher multi-hop graph queries with native HNSW vector similarity search using the <=> operator and BM25 inverted index text searches using the @@ operator in a single local binary file. Nodes follow a hierarchical schema comprising Document, Chunk, and Entity labels. Edges include [:HAS_CHUNK] linking documents to chunks, [:CONTAINS] linking chunks to extracted entities, and [:RELATION {type: ...}] linking entities together for multi-hop graph traversals. Because all indices share the same transactional storage layer, hybrid vector-graph queries execute with sub-millisecond latency.

corpus.title: FastEmbed Quantized Embeddings and Cross-Encoder Reranking
corpus.text: FastEmbed provides CPU-quantized dense and sparse vector generation without requiring GPU hardware. The default dense model is BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5, generating 384-dimensional normalized vector embeddings optimized for cosine similarity. For precision stage-3 reranking, the engine integrates BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3 in an INT8 quantized ONNX format from onnx-community/bge-reranker-v2-m3-ONNX. This cross-encoder features an 8,192 token context window, 568 million parameters, and executes inference in under 100 milliseconds on CPU via dynamic token batch padding. The cross-encoder scores every candidate on its own chunk text only: graph triples are not appended to candidates, because they are identical for every candidate and could not change the ordering. Paths traversed in LatticeDB from the entities of the final chunks are instead linearized into triples formatted as 'source --[relation type]--> target' and sent to the generation prompt.

corpus.title: GLiNER Zero-Shot Named Entity Recognition and Triples
corpus.text: The knowledge extraction pipeline employs GLiNER (Generalist and Lightweight Model for Named Entity Recognition). By default, the system loads fastino/GLiNER2.5-Decide as an efficient in-process extractor and falls back to urchade/gliner_small-v2.1 when that model is unavailable. GLiNER extracts domain entities corresponding to predefined labels including person, organization, technology, concept, algorithm, database, and protocol. Following entity extraction, the EntityExtractor extracts relation triples using sentence-level co-occurrence heuristics: when two entities co-occur within the same sentence, a [:RELATION] edge is created between their respective nodes in LatticeDB, with a relationship type built from the two entity types, such as CO_OCCURS_IN_TECHNOLOGY_DATABASE. Extracted entities are tied to their originating text chunk through [:CONTAINS] edges, ensuring tight provenance tracking and citation grounding.

corpus.title: TypeSafe AI Jev System One Decision Architecture
corpus.text: TypeSafe AI Jev is a specialized System One decision model trained to provide fast, calibrated judgments rather than generating free-form conversational text. The pipeline utilizes three primary Jev primitives. First, the Choice primitive acts as a front-door router, classifying incoming prompts in 70 to 500 milliseconds into vector_exact, graph_relational, hybrid, chitchat, or massive_context routes. Second, the boolean Noul primitive serves as a context guardrail, evaluating retrieved candidate chunks in parallel and pruning tangential passages with relevance probability below 0.50. Third, the Score primitive evaluates content across ordered descriptive criteria, returning expected-value continuous scores and probability distributions. By decomposing complex workflows into small typed judgments, Jev ensures deterministic control, low token usage, and sub-second pipeline throughput.

corpus.title: Litestar and Granian Rust-Optimized Web Framework
corpus.text: The web API layer is built on Litestar 2.24+ and served by Granian, a high-performance HTTP server written in Rust that delivers 2 to 4 times the throughput of standard Python Uvicorn servers. All data transfer objects are defined as msgspec.Struct instances with rename='camel' to ensure zero-copy sub-millisecond JSON serialization. The service provides dual query APIs: a synchronous POST /api/v1/query endpoint and a streaming POST /api/v1/query/stream endpoint emitting typed Server-Sent Events (SSE) with stage, token, and done events for frontend telemetry. If a provider fails after its first token, the stream sends an error event before the final done event. Error handling complies with RFC 9457 Problem Details, and all logging and error responses pass through automated regex sanitizers to scrub API keys, tokens, and authorization headers before reaching the network.

corpus.text:
# System Architecture & Technical Design

This document details the architectural principles, subsystems, and execution lifecycle of the **`lattice-rag`** engine.

## 1. Design Philosophy: The In-Process Paradigm

Traditional RAG and GraphRAG architectures introduce severe performance and cost bottlenecks:
- **Network Boundaries:** Hitting remote vector databases (Pinecone, Qdrant) over HTTP incurs 30–100ms per search.
- **Heavy Infrastructure Footprint:** JVM-based graph servers (Neo4j) consume gigabytes of memory and require dedicated cloud clusters.
- **Uncontrolled Context Windows:** Shoveling raw retrieved text into frontier LLMs inflates generation costs and increases hallucination surface.

`lattice-rag` adopts an **in-process, single-binary architecture**:
1. All graph nodes, edges, HNSW vector indices, and BM25 inverted indices reside inside a **single local file** (`data/lattice_rag.db`) managed by **LatticeDB**.
2. All embeddings and entity extractions run locally on **CPU** using quantized ONNX models via **FastEmbed** and **GLiNER2.5-Decide**.
3. Small, calibrated "System One" decision models (**TypeSafe AI Jev**) act as front-door traffic controllers and context guardrails, reducing token expenditures.

corpus.text:
## 2. End-to-End Query Execution Lifecycle

The following sequence diagram illustrates the lifecycle of a user query through the system:

## 3. Subsystem Breakdown

### 3.1 Web Server & API Layer (Litestar + Granian + msgspec)
- **Granian ASGI Server:** Multi-threaded Rust HTTP engine running on Python 3.12 without the overhead of standard Python web servers.
- **Litestar Framework:** Employs explicit parameter markers (`JSONBody`, `FromQuery`, `FromPath`) and DTO architectures.
- **msgspec Structs:** All request/response schemas use strict `msgspec.Struct` with `rename="camel"`, outperforming Pydantic by 2–4x in serialization speed.
- **Interactive Documentation:** Native **Scalar** OpenAPI interface rendered directly at `/schema/scalar`.

corpus.title: System Architecture & Technical Design: 3.2 System 1 Decision Routing (TypeSafe AI Jev)
corpus.text:
### 3.2 System 1 Decision Routing (TypeSafe AI Jev)
Instead of invoking large generative models for intent recognition, `lattice-rag` uses **TypeSafe AI Jev**:
- **Front-Door Router (`routing/router.py`):**
  Uses the `Choice` primitive to classify queries into:
  - `vector_exact`: Direct factual lookups and code definitions.
  - `graph_relational`: Questions requiring multi-step relational hops across entities.
  - `hybrid`: Broad semantic queries needing both text context and relational graph structure.
  - `chitchat`: Greetings and pleasantries. Messages made up entirely of small talk ("hi!", "thanks a lot", "what can you do?") skip the Jev call through a deterministic fast path; a question that merely contains such a word ("How does HNSW help recall?") is always routed by Jev.
  - `massive_context`: Cross-corpus summarizations requiring 1M token analysis.
- **Context Guardrail (`routing/guardrail.py`):**
  Uses the boolean `Noul` primitive to batch-score retrieved chunks against the user query, pruning irrelevant or tangential passages. It returns a per-request `GuardrailResult(chunks, low_grounding)`; when no chunk passes, the answer is generated without evidence, flagged `lowGrounding: true` in the response, and never cached. If Noul itself cannot run, the candidates pass through unchecked and the answer is an Unverified Answer (`unverified: true`), also never cached; the same applies when routing falls back to `hybrid`, and when a Tier 1 near-duplicate is found but its Noul equivalence check cannot run (the answer is recomputed rather than served). In mock-key mode the router and guardrail are not called at all. An optional `RerankScoreGate` (`GUARDRAIL_SKIP_RERANK_SCORE`, off by default) keeps chunks whose cross-encoder score clears the value without asking Noul; it is enabled only with Live Tier evidence (production-readiness §6).

corpus.title: System Architecture & Technical Design: 3.3 Storage Engine (LatticeDB)
corpus.text:
### 3.3 Storage Engine (LatticeDB)
- Embedded single-file property-graph engine (`data/lattice_rag.db`).
- **Unified Querying:**
  - HNSW vector similarity search (`<=>` operator) across 384-dimensional dense vectors.
  - BM25 full-text inverted index (`@@` operator) on text content.
  - Sub-millisecond graph traversals using native C bindings.

### 3.4 3-Stage Hybrid Retrieval Pipeline
1. **Stage 1 (Vector Candidate Recall):** The query embedding computed once during triage is reused; LatticeDB executes HNSW vector search and BM25 search, combining results via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) into `top_k + 3` candidates (`RERANK_HEADROOM`). Each candidate keeps its `doc_id` and `position` for citations.
2. **Stage 2 (Relational Traversal):** Runs after Stage 3 and the context guardrail. It takes entity anchors only from the final chunks (those that survived reranking and the guardrail), so the LLM never sees relations reachable only from rejected candidates, and walks LatticeDB edges in-process for 1 hop (2 for `graph_relational`). The budget (25) caps nodes and edges separately; reaching either cap ends the whole traversal, and an edge is kept only with both endpoints. This is a pointer walk through the LatticeDB transaction API, not a Cypher query.
3. **Stage 3 (Precision Reranking):** The INT8 ONNX cross-encoder (`bge-reranker-v2-m3`) scores **every** Stage 1 candidate on its own chunk text and keeps the top `top_k` (5, or 12 for `massive_context`). Graph triples are not appended to candidates: they are identical for every candidate, so they could not change the ordering. They go to the LLM prompt instead. Each candidate costs about 100 ms on CPU, which is why the headroom is small.

corpus.title: System Architecture & Technical Design: 3.5 Multi-Tier Caching & Circuit Breaker
corpus.text:
### 3.5 Multi-Tier Caching & Circuit Breaker

`ResilientSynthesizer` (`generation/resilient_synthesizer.py`) is the single generation path for both `RAGOrchestrator.run()` and `stream_query()`. It owns one `pybreaker` circuit breaker around Groq, paired with a 3-tier cascade:

- **Tier 1 (Semantic Vector Cache & Primary Groq):** Evaluates incoming query against in-memory query embeddings. If cosine similarity $\ge 0.90$, Jev's `Noul` primitive verifies semantic equivalence before the cached answer is returned. Standard non-cached queries route to primary **GroqCloud** (`GROQ_MODEL`). Only answers from the primary provider that were grounded in guardrail-approved evidence are cached.
- **Tier 2 (Circuit Breaker & Cascade 1 Fallback):** The breaker records every Groq outcome from both the buffered and streaming paths (`fail_max=3`, `reset_timeout=30s`). A Groq call that ends in an error counts as one failure. The Groq SDK and `GroqSynthesizer` retry HTTP 429 internally first, so a rate-limited call only counts once its retries are exhausted. Client disconnects (`asyncio.CancelledError`) are not counted. After 3 consecutive failures the circuit opens and Groq is skipped in favour of **Gemini** (`GEMINI_MODEL`) until the reset timeout lets a probe through. `massive_context` reverses the provider order: Gemini first, then Groq under the same breaker, then the FAQ. An answer from any provider other than the route's primary (Groq, or Gemini on `massive_context`) or from the FAQ is marked `degraded: true`.
- **Tier 3 (Cascade 2 Offline FAQ Hash):** If both LLM providers fail, the system returns the closest pre-computed answer from the Redis hash (`cache:fallback:queries`, seeded from `fallback_queries.json`). This answer is for the closest *seeded* question, not necessarily the one asked, so it is always marked degraded.
- **Streaming:** The cascade only moves to the next provider while nothing has been emitted. If a provider fails after its first token, the stream sends an `error` event and ends with `done` (`degraded: true`) rather than appending a second provider's answer.

### 3.6 Keeping CPU Work Off the Event Loop
Embedding, reranking, GLiNER extraction and LatticeDB reads and writes run in worker threads via `asyncio.to_thread()`, so the Litestar event loop keeps serving other requests. ONNX Runtime releases the GIL during inference, so the heaviest work (embedding and reranking) runs in parallel with request handling, without the pickling and model-reload cost of a process pool.

corpus.title: Storage Engine & Graph Schema (LatticeDB)
corpus.text:
# Storage Engine & Graph Schema (LatticeDB)

`lattice-rag` uses **LatticeDB** (v0.15+), an embedded, serverless, single-file property-graph database. It acts as an in-process SQLite for connected graph, vector, and full-text data.

## 1. Graph Data Model

The graph follows a **Hierarchical Document-Chunk-Entity** architecture:

### Node Labels & Properties

| Label | Properties | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `:Document` | `doc_id` (str), `title` (str) | Top-level document container. |
| `:Chunk` | `text` (str), `position` (int), `doc_id` (str), `embedding` (vector[384]) | Text segment with dense ONNX embedding and BM25 index. |
| `:Entity` | `name` (str), `entity_type` (str) | Extracted semantic entity (e.g. `LatticeDB`, `FastEmbed`). Entities carry no vector; retrieval reaches them through `CONTAINS` edges from chunks. |

corpus.title: Storage Engine & Graph Schema (LatticeDB): Edge Relationships
corpus.text:
### Edge Relationships

| Edge | Source $\to$ Target | Properties | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `HAS_CHUNK` | `:Document` $\to$ `:Chunk` | — | Preserves document hierarchy and reading order. |
| `CONTAINS` | `:Chunk` $\to$ `:Entity` | — | Grounding link tying entities to their exact source passage. |
| `RELATION` | `:Entity` $\to$ `:Entity` | `type` (str) | Semantic multi-hop relationship extracted by GLiNER. |

### Ingest Validation & Entity Identity

`ingest_document_bundle` validates the whole Document Bundle before it opens the write transaction, so a rejected bundle writes nothing:

- Every chunk embedding must have the store's `vector_dimensions`, or `EmbeddingDimensionError` is raised. A mismatch used to be skipped silently, which left chunks invisible to vector search.
- Each `(chunk_ref, entities, relations)` entry must name its chunk by index into the bundle's chunk list. An out-of-range or non-integer reference raises `UnresolvedChunkReferenceError`; it is never attributed to another chunk. `ingest_entities(chunk_id, ...)` raises the same error when `chunk_id` is not a stored Chunk.

Both are `IngestValidationError` subclasses; the ingest endpoint returns `422` and `lattice-rag ingest` exits with the message.

An Entity's identity is its **name plus type**, normalized by `entity_key()` (trimmed, internal whitespace collapsed, case-folded) both in the canonical-entity cache and inside the transaction. `Mercury`/`planet` and `Mercury`/`element` are two nodes; `LatticeDB`/`database` and ` latticedb`/`Database` are one. Relation endpoints carry only a name, so they resolve against the same chunk's entities first, then entities earlier in the same document; they never resolve by bare name across the whole graph.

corpus.title: Storage Engine & Graph Schema (LatticeDB): 2. Indices & Search Operations
corpus.text:
## 2. Indices & Search Operations

LatticeDB supports three native search modalities in a single file:

### 2.1 HNSW Vector Similarity Search
Only chunks have 384-dimensional dense vectors, generated by FastEmbed (`BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5`). Ingestion does not embed entities.

Databases seeded before this change may still hold entity vectors in the same HNSW index. `LatticeStore.vector_search` over-fetches (`max(3 * top_k, 20)`), drops nodes without chunk text, and widens the fetch (x4 per round, up to 4,096) until it has `top_k` chunks or the index is exhausted. Re-seed such a database to reclaim the index space.

- **Querying:**
  ```python
  raw_results = db.vector_search(query_embedding, k=10)
  ```
  Returns `List[VectorSearchResult]` with `node_id` and L2 distance in sub-millisecond time.
- **Scoring:** Converted to similarity via:
  $$\text{Score} = \frac{1}{1 + \text{distance}}$$

corpus.title: Storage Engine & Graph Schema (LatticeDB): 2.2 BM25 Full-Text Inverted Index
corpus.text:
### 2.2 BM25 Full-Text Inverted Index
Configured during database initialization:
```python
db.create_node_fts_index("Chunk", "text")
db.create_node_fts_index("Entity", "name")
```
- **Querying:**
  ```python
  raw_results = db.fts_search("Chunk", "text", query_text, limit=10)
  ```
  Returns BM25-ranked relevance scores for exact keyword and term matching.

### 2.3 Document Equality Index
`LatticeStore` creates an equality index on `Document.doc_id` at startup (building it backfills an existing database):
```python
db.create_node_property_index("Document", "doc_id")
txn.find_nodes_by_label_property("Document", "doc_id", doc_id)
```
The duplicate-document check on ingest and document delete both use it, so neither scans every Document.

corpus.title: Storage Engine & Graph Schema (LatticeDB): 2.4 Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
corpus.text:
### 2.4 Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
Vector similarity and BM25 search results are fused using standard RRF ($k=60$):
$$\text{RRF}(d) = \sum_{m \in \{\text{vector}, \text{bm25}\}} \frac{1}{60 + \text{rank}_m(d)}$$

## 3. Transaction & Commit Semantics

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Explicit Commit Requirement:**  
> In LatticeDB, write transactions (`with db.write() as txn:`) **default to rollback on context exit**. You must explicitly invoke `txn.commit()` before exiting the block:

```python
with db.write() as txn:
    doc = txn.create_node(labels=["Document"], properties={"doc_id": "1", "title": "Guide"})
    chunk = txn.create_node(labels=["Chunk"], properties={"text": "Content", "position": 0})
    txn.set_vector(chunk.id, "embedding", embedding_array)
    txn.create_edge(doc.id, chunk.id, "HAS_CHUNK")
    
    # CRITICAL: Commit transaction
    txn.commit()
```

corpus.title: Storage Engine & Graph Schema (LatticeDB): 3.1 Document Delete
corpus.text:
### 3.1 Document Delete
`LatticeStore.delete_document(doc_id)` runs in one write transaction. It removes the Document, its Chunks (with their vectors and BM25 entries), every edge on those nodes, and each Entity that no remaining Chunk `CONTAINS`; entities shared with other documents stay. LatticeDB's `delete_node` does not remove a node's edges, so the store deletes them explicitly first. Deleted entities leave the canonical-entity cache only after commit. `delete_document_in_txn(txn, doc_id)` exposes the same steps inside a caller's transaction. `DocumentIngester.delete` holds the ingest write lock while it runs and clears Tier 1 afterwards.

On the deployed instance, documents ingested or deleted at runtime are ephemeral ([ADR-0001](adr/0001-seeded-database-single-instance.md)).

## 4. Multi-Hop Relational Traversal

Multi-hop graph traversal pivots from Stage 1 entity anchors through `RELATION` edges:

```python
subgraph = store.traverse_from_entities(
    entity_ids=[anchor_id],
    max_hops=2,      # 1 hop for factual queries, 2 for relational
    budget=25        # Hard limit to guarantee < 1s latency
)
```

The traversal uses native C bindings (`txn.get_outgoing_edges()` and `txn.get_edge_property()`) to expand nodes along relationship paths in microseconds.

# API & DTO Contract Reference

`lattice-rag` provides a high-throughput REST and Server-Sent Events (SSE) streaming API built on **Litestar 2.24+** and **Granian**.

## 1. Interactive Documentation

An interactive Scalar OpenAPI documentation portal is automatically served at:
```
http://localhost:8000/schema/scalar
```

## 2. Endpoints Overview

| Method | Path | Auth | Request | Response Body | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `GET` | `/` | — | — | `text/html` | Studio SPA (or fallback landing page). |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/query` | rate-limited | `QueryRequest` | `QueryResponse` | Synchronous RAG query. |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/query/stream` | rate-limited | `QueryRequest` | `text/event-stream` | SSE stream of stage, token, error and done events. |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/ingest` | **admin** | `IngestRequest` | `IngestResponse` | Ingest a document. `409` if `documentId` already exists, unless `replace` is `true`: then the old version is deleted and the new one inserted in one transaction (a failed replace leaves the old version intact) and Tier 1 is cleared; `422` if the payload fails ingest validation (embedding dimension mismatch, unresolved chunk reference), in which case nothing is written. Runtime documents are ephemeral on the deployed instance (see §2.2). |
| `DELETE` | `/api/v1/documents/{documentId}` | **admin** | — | `204`, no body | Delete a document, its chunks and their edges, and every entity no remaining chunk references; then clear Tier 1. `404` if `documentId` is not stored. |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/graph/subgraph` | **admin** | query `limit` (1–500, default 50) | `SubgraphDTO` | Knowledge graph snapshot for the visualizer. |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/cache/stats` | **admin** | — | `CacheStatsResponse` | Tier 1 hit/miss counts and generation circuit-breaker state. |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/eval/jobs` | **admin** | query `dataset`, `baseline` (bare `*.json` names in the project root), `limit`, `use_temp_db` (default `true`) | `202` `EvalJobResponse` | Start an evaluation run in the background and return its handle immediately. `409` if a run is already in progress. |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/eval/jobs/{jobId}` | **admin** | — | `EvalJobResponse` | Status of an Eval Job and, once it has succeeded, its `EvalRunResponse` report. `404` for an unknown or expired handle. |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/benchmark/run` | **admin** | — | `BenchmarkRunResponse` | Retrieval-only latency benchmark (6 iterations, 2 warmup) with SLA checks. |
| `GET` | `/health` | — | — | `HealthResponse` | Health and configuration status. |

corpus.title: API & DTO Contract Reference: 2.1 Authentication & Limits
corpus.text:
### 2.1 Authentication & Limits
- **Public endpoints** (no key): `/`, `/health`, `POST /api/v1/query` and `POST /api/v1/query/stream`.
- **Admin-only endpoints**: `POST /api/v1/ingest`, `GET /api/v1/graph/subgraph`, `GET /api/v1/cache/stats`, `POST /api/v1/eval/jobs`, `GET /api/v1/eval/jobs/{jobId}` and `POST /api/v1/benchmark/run`.
- **Admin endpoints** require `X-Admin-Key: <ADMIN_API_KEY>`. A missing or wrong key returns `401`; if `ADMIN_API_KEY` is unset on the server, these endpoints are disabled. After 5 wrong keys within 5 minutes a client gets `429` for the rest of that window.
- **Query endpoints** are rate-limited per client (`QUERY_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE`, default 60) and return `429` when exceeded. Clients are identified by the socket peer, or by `X-Forwarded-For` when `TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS` is set (see `docs/deployment.md`).
- **Validation** failures return `400` problem details: `query` must be 1–2,000 characters, `text` 1–200,000, `documentId` must match `[A-Za-z0-9_.-]{1,128}`, and request bodies are capped at 1 MB.
- **Eval runs are serialized.** Only one Eval Job runs at a time per server process; a start request while one is running is rejected with `409` (it is not queued), so parallel requests cannot multiply judge and LLM API cost. Poll `GET /api/v1/eval/jobs/{jobId}` until `status` leaves `running`. The 20 most recent jobs are kept in memory and are lost on restart. A failed job's `error` carries only a reference id for the server logs. The `lattice-rag eval` CLI runs in its own process and does not go through this queue.
- **Unexpected errors** return `500` with a generic `detail` and a `requestId` to correlate with server logs; exception text is never returned.

corpus.title: API & DTO Contract Reference: 2.2 Runtime Documents Are Ephemeral
corpus.text:
### 2.2 Runtime Documents Are Ephemeral
The deployed instance serves a **Seeded Database** from the container's ephemeral disk ([ADR-0001](adr/0001-seeded-database-single-instance.md)). Documents added with `POST /api/v1/ingest` (and removals made with `DELETE /api/v1/documents/{documentId}`) apply only to the running instance and are lost on restart or redeploy. Durable content goes through `lattice-rag seed` at build time. Every `IngestResponse` repeats this in its `persistence` field.

## 3. Data Transfer Objects (DTOs)

All DTOs are declared as `msgspec.Struct` with `rename="camel"` for zero-copy JSON parsing.

corpus.text:
## 4. Server-Sent Events (SSE) Protocol

When querying `/api/v1/query/stream`, events are streamed in standard SSE format:

```http
POST /api/v1/query/stream HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{"query": "What is the relation between LatticeDB and FastEmbed?"}
```

**Stream Event Structure:** every `data:` line is a camelCase JSON object matching one of the `Stream*` DTOs in `api/dtos.py` (mirrored in `frontend/src/types.ts`).

```
event: stage
data: {"stage":"triage","status":"started"}

event: stage
data: {"stage":"retrieval","route":"hybrid"}

event: stage
data: {"stage":"generation","chunksCount":5}

event: token
data: {"delta":"LatticeDB"}

event: token
data: {"delta":" unites HNSW and BM25 in a single binary [Chunk 0]."}

event: done
data: {"answer":"LatticeDB unites ...","route":"hybrid","cached":false,"latencyMs":528.2,"sources":[...],"graphPath":{...},"timings":[...],"degraded":false,"lowGrounding":false,"unverified":false}
```

| Event | Payload | When |
|---|---|---|
| `stage` | `{stage, status?, route?, chunksCount?}` | A pipeline stage starts (`triage`, `cache_hit`, `chitchat`, `retrieval`, `generation`). |
| `token` | `{delta}` | Next piece of answer text. |
| `error` | `{detail}` | Generation stopped early (the provider failed after its first token), or the request failed (`detail` carries a reference id). |
| `done` | Same fields as `QueryResponse` | Final event of a completed stream. |

# Zero-Cost Production Deployment Guide

This guide details how to host and operate `lattice-rag` for **$0.00/month** in production without compromising on retrieval quality or downgrading our state-of-the-art **`bge-reranker-v2-m3`** cross-encoder.

## 1. Memory Architecture & The 512MB RAM Ceiling

During Phase 6 profiling, resident memory consumption across all pipeline subsystems was empirically benchmarked on macOS/Linux:

| Component | Resident Memory (RAM) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Base Python Runtime + Granian** | ~14 MB | In-process ASGI server overhead |
| **FastEmbed `bge-small-en-v1.5`** | ~289 MB | INT8 ONNX dense bi-encoder |
| **Cross-Encoder `bge-reranker-v2-m3`** | **1,176 MB (1.17 GB)** | SOTA multilingual cross-encoder (544MB ONNX weights expand to ~887MB during inference) |
| **LatticeDB + Caches** | ~35 MB | SQLite property graph + FTS5 indices + vector tables |
| **Total Peak Working Set** | **~1.51 GB** | Required allocation: **$\ge$ 2 GB RAM** |

> [!WARNING]
> **512MB Free Tier OOM Hazard:**
> Platforms offering only 512MB RAM (such as Render Free, Koyeb Free, or basic Hugging Face CPU Spaces) **will crash with an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) kill** when executing cross-encoder reranking. To maintain uncompromised retrieval precision, `lattice-rag` is deployed to free-tier environments providing **$\ge$ 2GB RAM**.

corpus.title: Zero-Cost Production Deployment Guide: Client identity behind reverse proxies (`TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS`)
corpus.text:
## Client identity behind reverse proxies (`TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS`)

The query rate limit (`QUERY_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE`) and the admin-key lockout both key on the client's address. `TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS` says how many reverse proxies sit between the client and the app:

| Value | Client identity | Use for |
|-------|-----------------|---------|
| `0` (default) | Socket peer; `X-Forwarded-For` is ignored | Direct exposure, local dev |
| `1` | Rightmost `X-Forwarded-For` entry | Cloud Run, a single nginx/Caddy, Cloudflare Tunnel |
| `N` | `N`th entry from the right | `N` proxies that each append to `X-Forwarded-For` |

Every proxy appends the address it received the request from, so entries to the left of the trusted ones were written by the client and are ignored. A header with fewer than `N` entries is not trusted and the socket peer is used.

Set the value to the real hop count. Too low, and every client behind the proxy shares one identity (one rate-limit budget, one lockout). Too high, and clients can choose their identity by sending their own `X-Forwarded-For`. `scripts/deploy_cloud_run.sh` sets `TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS=1`; override it (`TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS=2 ./scripts/deploy_cloud_run.sh ...`) when an external HTTPS load balancer fronts the service.

**Admin-key lockout.** A client that sends a wrong `X-Admin-Key` 5 times within 5 minutes gets `429` from the admin endpoints for the rest of that window, even with the right key. Other clients are unaffected, and a successful attempt clears the count. Counts are kept in process memory per server worker and reset on restart.

corpus.text:
## 5. Cold-Start Optimization

`lattice-rag`'s multi-stage `Dockerfile` incorporates two key production optimizations:
1. **Pre-Baked Model Weights**: ONNX weights for `bge-small-en-v1.5` and `bge-reranker-v2-m3` are downloaded during image creation (`docker build`), eliminating 600MB+ network pulls on container cold start.
2. **Pre-Seeded Database**: `lattice-rag seed` ingests the golden corpus at build time (it needs no API keys and skips documents that already exist), so the graph, HNSW and BM25 indexes are ready when the container starts.

The runtime stage runs as an unprivileged user (`uid 10001`), excludes compilers (dependencies are built in a separate stage), and declares a `HEALTHCHECK` on `/health`.

# Secret Security & Sensitivity Architecture

`lattice-rag` enforces a zero-trust credential security architecture to guarantee that API keys, authentication tokens, and private connection strings are never exposed in logs, error payloads, terminal outputs, or version control.

## 1. Multi-Layer Security Boundary

## 2. Git & Filesystem Hygiene

### 2.1 Git Boundary Protection
The `.gitignore` file enforces that secrets and database files can never be committed:
```gitignore
# Secrets and Environment Variables
.env
.env.*
!.env.example
apikeys.md
*.pem
*.key
secrets/

# Embedded Databases & Cache
data/
*.db
*.db-*
*.latticedb
```

A sanitized template (`.env.example`) is checked into git with documented variable names and blank values.

corpus.title: Secret Security & Sensitivity Architecture: 2.2 Automated Credential Migration (`setup-keys`)
corpus.text:
### 2.2 Automated Credential Migration (`setup-keys`)
Storing API keys in plain text files like `apikeys.md` is a common credential exposure hazard.

`lattice-rag` provides an automated, secure migration utility:
```bash
lattice-rag setup-keys
```

**What it does:**
1. Reads `apikeys.md` if present.
2. Extracts recognized keys (`TYPESAFE_API_KEY`, `GROQ_API_KEY`, `GEMINI_API_KEY`, `ADMIN_API_KEY`, `REDIS_URL`).
3. Appends the ones `.env` does not already define. `.env` is created with `0600` permissions from the start (`os.open(..., 0o600)`), not chmod-ed after the write.
4. Deletes `apikeys.md`. If no recognizable key was found, `apikeys.md` is left untouched so nothing is lost.

corpus.title: Secret Security & Sensitivity Architecture: 3. Runtime & Memory Protection
corpus.text:
## 3. Runtime & Memory Protection

### 3.1 `SecretStr` Type
API keys are never stored as plain strings in memory configurations. They are wrapped in `SecretStr`:

```python
from lattice_rag.security import SecretStr

key = SecretStr("sk-live_9876543210abcdef")

# __str__ and __repr__ return masked representations:
print(str(key))   # 'sk-****cdef'
print(repr(key))  # "SecretStr('sk-****cdef')"

# Raw access requires explicit call:
raw = key.get_secret_value()
```

Supported mask patterns:
- `sk-****{last_4}` (OpenAI, TypeSafe)
- `gsk_****{last_4}` (Groq)
- `AIza****{last_4}` (Google Gemini)
- `[REDACTED]` (General secrets)

corpus.title: Secret Security & Sensitivity Architecture: 3.2 Log Redaction
corpus.text:
### 3.2 Log Redaction
One pattern, `security.REDACT_PATTERN`, matches `sk-`, `gsk_` and `AIza` keys, bearer tokens, `token=` parameters and URI credentials (including password-only forms such as `redis://:secret@host`). It is applied at two points:
- **`RedactingFormatter`** renders every log line, then redacts the *whole rendered line*, tracebacks included. The web app installs it as Litestar's `standard` formatter, and the CLI installs it through `configure_logging()`.
- **`configure_structlog()`** routes `structlog` through stdlib logging, so structlog events (used by the routing, caching, generation and eval modules) pass through the same redacting formatter instead of printing directly.

`RedactingFilter` remains available for redacting a record's message and arguments before formatting. User queries are not logged at INFO level.

corpus.title: Secret Security & Sensitivity Architecture: 3.3 RFC 9457 Error Shielding
corpus.text:
### 3.3 RFC 9457 Error Shielding
Unexpected exceptions never reach clients verbatim. The global handler logs the sanitized exception server-side with a request id, and returns a generic `500` problem document that carries only that id (`requestId`). HTTP errors such as validation `400`s, `401`, `404` and `409` keep their normal problem-details responses. Mid-stream failures on `/api/v1/query/stream` are reported in-band as an SSE `error` event with the same kind of reference.

### 3.4 Access Control & Abuse Limits
- **Admin key:** `POST /api/v1/ingest`, `DELETE /api/v1/documents/{documentId}`, `GET /api/v1/graph/subgraph`, `GET /api/v1/cache/stats`, `/api/v1/eval/jobs` (start and status) and `POST /api/v1/benchmark/run` require an `X-Admin-Key` header matching `ADMIN_API_KEY` (constant-time comparison). The graph snapshot exposes the whole ingested knowledge graph and the cache stats expose operational state, so they are admin-only alongside the write and cost endpoints. With no `ADMIN_API_KEY` configured these endpoints reject every request (fail closed). A client that sends a wrong key 5 times within 5 minutes is locked out with `429` for the rest of that window; its key is not checked while locked, and other clients are unaffected.
- **Public endpoints:** `/`, `/api/v1/query`, `/api/v1/query/stream` and `/health` need no key, so the studio and uptime checks keep working. The studio's Full Graph view loads only once an admin key has been entered. The query endpoints are rate-limited per client (`QUERY_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE`, default 60).
- **Client identity:** the rate limit and the admin-key lockout identify clients by the socket peer. `X-Forwarded-For` is used only when `TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS` is set to N > 0, taking the Nth entry from the right, so client-forged entries to the left are ignored. See `docs/deployment.md`.
- **Input bounds:** queries are limited to 2,000 characters, documents to 200,000 characters, `documentId` to `[A-Za-z0-9_.-]{1,128}`, request bodies to 1 MB, and the graph `limit` to 1–500.
- **Eval files:** the eval endpoint only accepts bare `*.json` file names in the project root for `dataset` and `baseline`, so it cannot be pointed at arbitrary server paths.
- **CORS:** same-origin only unless `CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS` lists trusted origins.

corpus.title: Secret Security & Sensitivity Architecture: 3.5 Prompt-Injection Hardening
corpus.text:
### 3.5 Prompt-Injection Hardening
Ingested documents become evidence in LLM prompts. Both providers share one prompt (`generation/prompt.py`). A system message states that evidence and the question are untrusted data whose instructions must not be followed. The user message wraps each chunk in `<chunk>` tags inside `<evidence>`, and escapes `<` in evidence and the question so neither can close a block or inject a fake `<question>`. This reduces, but cannot eliminate, the risk; the admin key on `/ingest` controls who can add evidence in the first place.

### 3.6 Process-Level Isolation
Secrets are loaded strictly into memory from `.env` via `python-dotenv` at process startup. They are **never** passed as CLI arguments, preventing exposure in system process tables (`ps aux`) to other OS users.

## 4. CI/CD Protection
- **No Hardcoded Keys in CI:** Pull requests and automated eval workflows inject credentials via GitHub Actions Repository Secrets (`${{ secrets.TYPESAFE_API_KEY }}`).
- **Secret Scanning Test:** `tests/unit/test_security_audit.py::test_git_tracked_files_zero_secrets` scans every git-tracked file for live key patterns as part of the unit suite that CI runs on every push and PR.

# Production Latency, Throughput & Performance Profiling

This document outlines the empirical latency benchmarks, throughput metrics, resource profile, and architectural performance guarantees of the `lattice-rag` Hybrid GraphRAG engine.

## 1. Executive Summary & Dual-SLA Guarantees

Traditional GraphRAG architectures suffer from severe cloud latency inflation and high recurring costs caused by separate network hops between microservices (e.g., Pinecone/Weaviate for vectors, Neo4j for property graphs, and external reranker APIs). 

`lattice-rag` unifies **LatticeDB** (embedded property-graph + HNSW + BM25 in a single binary), **FastEmbed** (local CPU-quantized dense embeddings), and **INT8 ONNX `bge-reranker-v2-m3`** into an entirely in-process execution pipeline.

corpus.title: Production Latency, Throughput & Performance Profiling: Dual-SLA Production Enforcements
corpus.text:
### Dual-SLA Production Enforcements

| SLA Target | Target Threshold | Empirical Result ($p95$) | Status | Enforcement Mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Sub-Second Retrieval SLA** | Retrieval-only E2E $p95 < 1,000$ms | **812.6ms** | **[PASSED]** | `--sla-check` CLI & `BenchmarkEngine` |
| **Tier 1 Cache Latency SLA** | Exact-hit $p95 < 25$ms | **0.03ms** | **[PASSED]** | In-memory exact-match map |

**Scope of the numbers.** The default (zero-cost) benchmark measures *retrieval only*: Stage 1, Stage 2 and Stage 3, without Jev routing, the Noul guardrail or the LLM call, which all depend on external network latency. `lattice-rag benchmark --live` runs the full pipeline (bypassing the Tier 1 cache) and reports it as a separate scope. The Tier 1 SLA covers the exact-match path; the similarity-scan row excludes the Jev Noul verification call that a real fuzzy hit makes.

corpus.title: Production Latency, Throughput & Performance Profiling: 2. Empirical Benchmark Matrix
Production Latency, Throughput & Performance Profiling: Stage-by-Stage Architectural Breakdown
corpus.text:
### Stage-by-Stage Architectural Breakdown

1. **Tier 1 Cache (exact hit $p95 = 0.03$ms)**:
   - Exact (normalized) query strings resolve from an in-memory map without embedding the query.
   - Paraphrased queries ($\text{cosine} \ge 0.90$) are found by a vectorized NumPy dot product, then confirmed by a TypeSafe AI Jev Noul call. That network call dominates a real fuzzy hit and is excluded from the similarity-scan row.

2. **Stage 1: Hybrid Retrieval ($p95 = 7.2$ms)**:
   - Query embedding via FastEmbed (`BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5`, 384 dimensions). In the full pipeline this embedding is computed once during triage and reused here.
   - LatticeDB HNSW search and BM25 full-text search, merged with Reciprocal Rank Fusion ($k=60$) into `top_k + 3` candidates.

3. **Stage 2: Graph Traversal ($p95 = 1.7$ms)**:
   - Walks `:CONTAINS` edges from the Stage 1 chunks to their entities, then `:RELATION` edges up to 2 hops (budget 25 nodes), through LatticeDB's in-process transaction API.
   - Earlier versions of this benchmark passed entity ids where chunk ids were expected, so the traversal found no anchors and timed a no-op (about 0.3 ms). The figure above measures a real traversal.

4. **Stage 3: Cross-Encoder Reranking ($p95 = 293.7$ms for 3 chunks)**:
   - INT8 ONNX `BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3` scores each candidate's chunk text (`intra_op_num_threads=4`). Cost grows roughly linearly at about 100 ms per candidate on this CPU, which is why Stage 1 adds only 3 candidates of headroom.

5. **End-to-End, retrieval only ($p95 = 812.6$ms)**:
   - Stage 1 + Stage 2 + Stage 3 for `top_k=5` (8 reranked candidates), without routing, guardrail or generation.
   - The rerank stage dominates. Routing, the guardrail and the LLM call add network-bound latency on top; measure them with `--live`.

corpus.title: Production Latency, Throughput & Performance Profiling: Rerank headroom and `top_k` tuning (#20)
corpus.text:
### Rerank headroom and `top_k` tuning (#20)

`RERANK_HEADROOM` (3) and `top_k` (5, or 12 for `massive_context`) are changed only when the retrieval benchmark and the Hermetic Tier agree. Sweep of `RERANK_HEADROOM` on the 30-query Gold Set (macOS, CPU, real models, no keys; latencies are per query over the 26 non-chitchat queries, miss path = exact miss + embed + semantic scan + offline route + retrieval at `top_k=5`):

| Headroom | Hermetic recall (overall / multihop) | MRR overall | Miss path p50 / p95 | Retrieval `top_k=12` p50 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 (shipped) | 1.000 / 1.000 | 0.978 | 893 / 1069 ms | 1120 ms |
| 2 | 0.986 / 0.944 | 0.978 | 1222 / 1362 ms | 1771 ms |
| 1 | 0.986 / 0.944 | 0.978 | 990 / 1203 ms | 1630 ms |
| 0 | 0.986 / 0.944 | 0.978 | 842 / 1222 ms | 1649 ms |

Every value under 3 loses a multihop Gold Passage, and the latency saving is smaller than run-to-run noise on a shared CPU (the eval chunks are long, so the cost per candidate varies). Both stay unchanged. On the cache paths, an exact Tier 1 hit costs under 0.1 ms, and a lookup that is not exact costs the query embedding plus the cosine scan (about 10–20 ms) before any routing starts.

The optional rerank-score Noul skip (`GUARDRAIL_SKIP_RERANK_SCORE`) affects only the guardrail, which the retrieval-only benchmark does not run. It ships off; see [production-readiness.md, section 6](production-readiness.md#rerank-score-noul-skip-off-by-default) for how to enable it.

## 3. Resource & Memory Footprint

| Metric | Profile | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| **RAM Footprint (Cold)** | $\sim 85$ MB | Litestar + Granian base server. |
| **RAM Footprint (Warm ML)** | $\sim 420$ MB | FastEmbed embeddings, GLiNER NER model, and INT8 ONNX cross-encoder loaded in memory. |
| **Container Memory Target** | $1,024$ MB (1 GB) | Safely runs inside free/low-tier container environments (e.g. Render, Railway, Fly.io, Google Cloud Run). |
| **Database Storage Footprint** | $\sim 65$ MB | LatticeDB stores chunks, 384-dim HNSW vector indices, BM25 inverted index, and property graph nodes/edges in a single file (`data/lattice_rag.db`). |

corpus.title: Production Latency, Throughput & Performance Profiling: 4. In-Process vs Cloud-Hosted Vector/Graph Architecture
corpus.text:
## 4. In-Process vs Cloud-Hosted Vector/Graph Architecture

| Dimension | `lattice-rag` (In-Process) | Traditional Cloud GraphRAG Stack |
|---|---|---|
| **Architecture** | Single container, single process | App + Pinecone/Weaviate + Neo4j Aura + Cohere Rerank API |
| **Network Hops** | 0 external network hops | 4–6 HTTPS roundtrips per query |
| **Retrieval Latency** | **$813$ms** ($p95$, retrieval only) | $1,800$ms – $3,500$ms ($p95$) |
| **Monthly Cloud Cost** | **$0.00** | $150 – $800+ / month (minimum SaaS tiers) |
| **Deployment Complexity** | Single Docker container (`docker run`) | Multi-tenant VPC peering, secrets management, distributed schema migrations |
| **Data Privacy** | In-process, single host | Customer text sent to multiple 3rd-party vector/graph clouds |

queries.query: How does LatticeDB combine HNSW vector similarity with BM25 text search in a single binary?
queries.reference_answer: LatticeDB unites native HNSW vector similarity search (the <=> operator) and BM25 inverted index text search (the @@ operator), together with Cypher multi-hop graph queries, in a single local binary file.

gold_passages.text: It uniquely unites Cypher multi-hop graph queries with native HNSW vector similarity search using the <=> operator and BM25 inverted index text searches using the @@ operator in a single local binary file.

queries.query: What edge relationships link Document, Chunk, and Entity nodes in LatticeDB?
queries.reference_answer: Documents link to Chunks through [:HAS_CHUNK] edges, Chunks link to the Entities extracted from them through [:CONTAINS] edges, and Entities link to each other through [:RELATION {type: ...}] edges.

gold_passages.text: Nodes follow a hierarchical schema comprising Document, Chunk, and Entity labels. Edges include [:HAS_CHUNK] linking documents to chunks, [:CONTAINS] linking chunks to extracted entities, and [:RELATION {type: ...}] linking entities together for multi-hop graph traversals.
